analogy.p: Imagine you pour a drink mix into a jug of water and keep adding more mix until some powder stays at the bottom: you know the water cannot take any more, just as extra copper oxide shows that all the acid has been used up. Pouring the jug through a sieve keeps the lumps behind (the residue) and lets the drink through (the filtrate). Boiling off a bit of water and leaving it to stand is like making sugar crystals on a string. It breaks down because the acid and oxide really react to form a new substance (a salt) rather than simply mixing, whereas a drink mix only dissolves.

bullets: A **soluble** substance dissolves in a solvent (here water) to form a solution; an **insoluble** substance does not dissolve and stays as a solid.

Common solubility rules for GCSE: all common sodium, potassium and ammonium salts are soluble; all nitrates are soluble; most chlorides are soluble (except silver and lead chloride); most sulfates are soluble (except lead, barium and calcium sulfate).
Most carbonates and hydroxides are insoluble, except those of sodium, potassium and ammonium; this is why insoluble carbonates and hydroxides can be used as the excess solid.
The salt solution that is made is called the **filtrate** once the excess solid has been filtered out.
Copper(II) sulfate, zinc sulfate, magnesium chloride and sodium nitrate are all soluble salts you could be asked to prepare.
Link to topics: solubility rules are also used when you make an insoluble salt by precipitation and when you test for ions in 4.8 (Chemical analysis).
core.h: What is a salt and which salts are soluble?
core.p: A **salt** is the compound formed when the hydrogen ions of an acid are replaced by a metal ion or by the ammonium ion. When an acid reacts with a base, an alkali, a metal or a metal carbonate, a salt is always one of the products. This practical makes a **soluble salt**, meaning a salt that dissolves in water, so that it ends up dissolved in the reaction mixture and can be separated from any leftover solid by filtering. It is only possible to make a salt by this method if the salt is soluble; if the salt was insoluble it would stay mixed up with the excess solid and could not be filtered away.

bullets: **Acid + metal → salt + hydrogen** (e.g. zinc + sulfuric acid → zinc sulfate + hydrogen).
**Acid + metal oxide → salt + water** (e.g. copper oxide + sulfuric acid → copper sulfate + water).
**Acid + metal hydroxide → salt + water** (a neutralisation, e.g. zinc hydroxide + hydrochloric acid → zinc chloride + water).
**Acid + metal carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide** (e.g. magnesium carbonate + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + water + carbon dioxide).
Metal oxides, metal hydroxides and metal carbonates are all called **bases** if they neutralise an acid; a base that dissolves in water is an **alkali**.
Because oxides give no gas, the only sign that a reaction has happened is that the black solid disappears and the solution changes colour, which is why you add solid until some remains undissolved.
Link to topics: these are the same reactions as in 'Reactions of acids with metals' and in the neutralisation work in 4.4.2.
core.h: The general equations: acid plus solid gives salt
core.p: Every method of making a soluble salt from an acid relies on one of four general reactions. In each case the acid is **neutralised** or used up, and a metal salt is formed along with one or two other products. Learning these four word equations lets you work out the products for any acid and any solid in the exam, because the pattern never changes. The name of the other products also tells you what you would observe: a metal makes hydrogen gas, a carbonate makes carbon dioxide gas, and an oxide or hydroxide makes only water so there is no fizzing.

bullets: **Hydrochloric acid, HCl → chloride** (e.g. MgCl2, ZnCl2, CuCl2).
**Nitric acid, HNO3 → nitrate** (e.g. Zn(NO3)2, Cu(NO3)2, NaNO3).
**Sulfuric acid, H2SO4 → sulfate** (e.g. CuSO4, ZnSO4, MgSO4).
The metal part of the name comes from the solid: copper oxide → copper salt; zinc carbonate → zinc salt.
Sulfuric acid is **dibasic**, so it needs two hydroxide-type units: this is why the equation for hydroxides and sulfuric acid needs balancing (2NaOH + H2SO4 → Na2SO4 + 2H2O).
Ammonia solution is an alkali which forms **ammonium salts**, for example ammonia + nitric acid → ammonium nitrate, an important fertiliser containing nitrogen.
Phosphoric acid can also be used to make phosphates in industry, but you only need the three acids above in the practical.
core.h: Naming the salt from the acid used
core.p: The second part of the salt's name comes from the acid you used, and the first part comes from the metal in the solid. This is a very common one-mark question, so it is worth knowing by heart. Hydrochloric acid always makes **chlorides**, nitric acid always makes **nitrates** and sulfuric acid always makes **sulfates**. For example, magnesium oxide and sulfuric acid make magnesium sulfate, but magnesium oxide and nitric acid make magnesium nitrate. The metal name is taken from the solid, so zinc carbonate gives a zinc salt.

bullets: **Dilute sulfuric acid** (about 1 mol/dm3), roughly 20 to 40 cm3, measured with a measuring cylinder and poured into a beaker.
**Copper(II) oxide**, a black powder, added using a spatula in small amounts.
A **Bunsen burner**, tripod, gauze and heatproof mat, or an electric hotplate or water bath, to warm the acid gently.
A **glass rod** to stir so that the powder reacts with the acid quickly.
A **filter funnel** and **filter paper** held over a conical flask or beaker to separate the excess solid.
An **evaporating basin** to heat the filtrate and evaporate some of the water.
A **watch glass or crystallising dish** for the solution to cool and crystallise, and filter paper or a warm oven to dry the crystals.
Safety: wear **eye protection**; dilute sulfuric acid and copper sulfate are irritants and copper sulfate is harmful if swallowed.
core.h: Required practical: the equipment and chemicals
core.p: The standard version of this practical makes copper sulfate crystals from copper oxide and dilute sulfuric acid, though your teacher might use zinc oxide, magnesium oxide or a carbonate instead. You are expected to know what each piece of equipment is for, since examiners ask you to name it or to say why it is used. The acid is warmed so that the reaction goes faster, but it must not be boiled. The insoluble solid is added in small portions with stirring until no more reacts, which is shown when some solid is left at the bottom of the beaker.

bullets: Equation: **CuO + H2SO4 → CuSO4 + H2O**; the ionic form is CuO + 2H+ → Cu2+ + H2O.
Warming increases the rate of reaction because the particles move faster and collide more often and with more energy.
Add the solid in **small portions** and stir after each so you can see when the oxide stops dissolving.
The solution turning blue is the evidence that copper sulfate has formed; the leftover black solid is the unreacted copper oxide.
If you are using a **carbonate**, add it slowly because it fizzes as carbon dioxide is released and the mixture can froth over the top of the beaker.
If you are using a **metal** such as zinc or magnesium, hydrogen gas bubbles are given off; the reaction is complete when the bubbling stops and metal is left.
Do not let the acid boil as it can spit out and cause burns.
core.h: Step 1: react the acid with the excess solid
core.p: Warm the dilute sulfuric acid in a beaker, taking care not to let it boil. Add a small amount of copper oxide with a spatula and stir with the glass rod. The black powder disappears as it reacts and the colourless acid turns **blue** as copper sulfate forms. Keep adding the oxide a little at a time until no more will dissolve and some black solid stays at the bottom of the beaker even after stirring. This means the oxide is in **excess**, so all of the acid has been used up, which is exactly what we want before we filter.

bullets: Excess solid ensures that **all of the acid reacts**, so no acid is left in the salt solution.
The excess is **insoluble**, so it does not dissolve and can be separated by filtering.
Mark-scheme phrase: 'to make sure all the acid has reacted' or 'so that the acid is the limiting reactant'.
If the acid was the excess reactant, the crystals would be impure because acid would remain in the solution.
With a soluble alkali (such as sodium hydroxide) you cannot use this method; you need a titration and an indicator to find the exact neutralisation point.
You know there is excess when solid remains after stirring for a minute or two and the effervescence (for carbonates) has stopped.
Link to topics: 'limiting reactant' in the quantitative chemistry topic means the reactant that is used up first; here it is the acid.
core.h: Why use an excess of the insoluble solid?
core.p: This is the most important 'why' in the whole practical. If you added too little solid, some of the acid would be left in your final solution and the crystals would be contaminated. Because the solid is **insoluble**, adding extra is harmless: whatever is not needed to react simply sits at the bottom and is removed by filtering. This is the clever reason why an insoluble solid is chosen rather than a soluble alkali, because with an alkali you cannot see when it is exactly neutral and you cannot filter off the excess.

bullets: **Residue** = the solid left on the filter paper (unreacted copper oxide); **filtrate** = the liquid that passes through (blue copper sulfate solution).
The filtrate should be clear and blue; if it looks cloudy, the filter paper has torn or some solid got through, so filter again.
Do not fill the filter paper above its rim, otherwise solid can run down the side.
Filtering separates an insoluble solid from a liquid because the solid particles are larger than the pores in the paper.
The residue can be washed with distilled water and the washings added to the filtrate to improve yield.
Link to topics: filtration is one of the separation techniques in 'Chemical analysis and the Earth's resources', along with crystallisation, distillation and chromatography.
core.h: Step 2: filter to remove the excess solid
core.p: Fold a piece of filter paper into a cone, place it in the filter funnel and hold the funnel over a conical flask or a beaker. Pour the mixture through the funnel. The salt solution passes through the tiny holes in the filter paper because the dissolved particles are very small, while the **excess solid** is too big to pass through and stays behind in the paper as the **residue**. The solution that goes through is the **filtrate** and it contains the dissolved salt. Rinse the beaker with a little distilled water and pour that through too, so you do not lose any salt.

bullets: Evaporation removes some of the **solvent** (water) so the solution becomes concentrated.
Test for the crystallisation point: remove a drop on a glass rod and let it cool; if crystals appear on the rod, stop heating.
Do not evaporate to dryness because the salt would be a powder rather than crystals and the heating can make it spit out and give burns.

Many salts such as copper sulfate form **hydrated crystals** (CuSO4.5H2O) which contain water of crystallisation; heating strongly drives this water off and the blue crystals turn into white anhydrous powder.
A slower evaporation gives larger and neater crystals, a quicker one gives lots of small ones.
Heat gently, keep the basin away from your face and use heatproof gloves or tongs when moving it.
core.h: Step 3: evaporate part of the water
core.p: Pour the filtrate into an evaporating basin and heat it gently with a Bunsen burner, hotplate or over a water bath. Heating makes the water evaporate and the solution becomes more concentrated. You do **not** heat until all the water has gone. Instead, you heat until about half the volume remains, or until the **point of crystallisation** is reached, which you can check by dipping a clean glass rod into the solution and seeing whether small crystals form on the rod as it cools. At this point the solution is **saturated** at that temperature, meaning it cannot hold any more dissolved salt when it cools.

bullets: Cooling lowers the solubility of the salt, so the extra solute comes out of solution as crystals.
Crystals should be filtered or removed with a spatula, rinsed with a very small amount of ice cold distilled water (a lot would dissolve them) and dried.
Dry between sheets of filter paper or in a desiccator or warm oven, but not at a high temperature or the water of crystallisation could be lost.
The crystals can be examined with a hand lens or microscope; copper sulfate forms blue, rhomboid-shaped crystals.
Copper sulfate pentahydrate is **CuSO4.5H2O**; the **.5H2O** shows five water molecules for each copper sulfate in the crystal.
Evaporating the rest of the water would give a powder rather than crystals.
Keep the crystals in a labelled container.
core.h: Step 4: leave to cool and crystallise, then dry
core.p: Leave the concentrated solution somewhere warm and still to cool and allow the water to evaporate slowly over a day or so. As the solution cools, the salt becomes less soluble and crystals begin to form. Larger crystals grow when cooling is slow. When enough crystals have formed, pour off the remaining liquid or filter the mixture, then rinse the crystals with a little cold distilled water to remove any surface solution. Finally, pat them dry gently with filter paper or leave them in a warm place such as a warm oven. The final product is a **pure, dry sample** of the soluble salt.

bullets: **moles = mass (g) ÷ relative formula mass (Mr)**; **mass = moles × Mr**.
**Percentage yield = (actual yield ÷ theoretical yield) × 100**.
Mr of the hydrated crystals CuSO4.5H2O = 159.5 + (5 × 18) = 249.5.
Reasons yield is below 100%: some salt stays in solution (the mother liquor), some is left on the filter paper or glassware, and transfer losses.
A yield above 100% usually means the crystals were not dry or contain impurities.
Atom economy is a separate idea: it is the proportion of the reactant mass that ends up as the desired product.
core.p: Once you have a balanced symbol equation you can predict the maximum mass of salt you could make, called the **theoretical yield**, and compare it with the mass actually made to find the **percentage yield**. The mole ratios come directly from the equation. For CuO + H2SO4 → CuSO4 + H2O the ratio is 1 : 1 : 1 : 1, so moles of salt equals moles of the limiting reactant. Mass is found with **mass = moles × Mr**, and moles with **moles = mass ÷ Mr**. The yield is nearly always less than 100% because some product is lost in filtering, transfers and in solution that remains.

bullets: Hazard: dilute sulfuric acid is an irritant → wear goggles, wash splashes immediately with plenty of water.
Hazard: hot solution and glassware → let the apparatus cool, use tongs and a heatproof mat.
Hazard: spitting when evaporating → heat gently, stop before dryness, keep face away.
Hazard: copper sulfate is harmful if swallowed and toxic to aquatic life → wash hands, and dispose of solid and solutions as instructed, not down the sink.
Hazard: fizzing carbonate can spill over → add slowly.
Hazard: hydrogen is flammable → no naked flames near the reaction if a metal is used (but heating must be controlled and not near the gas).
Risk assessments tie each hazard to a control measure; use the word 'because'.
core.p: Required practicals always assess risk. You should be able to name a hazard and the precaution that reduces it. Dilute sulfuric acid is an **irritant**, copper sulfate is **harmful** and an environmental hazard, hot equipment can burn you, and boiling or spitting liquids can burn skin and eyes. A good answer links the hazard to the control measure with a reason, as in 'wear eye protection because the acid can irritate or damage eyes'.

bullets: Insoluble base + acid → use **excess** and **filter**.
Soluble alkali + acid → use a **pipette**, a **burette** and an **indicator** to find the end point, then repeat without the indicator.
Common indicators: litmus, universal indicator, methyl orange and phenolphthalein; the colour change shows the end point.
The salt solution is then crystallised the same way as before.
The method is the titration required practical.
Sodium nitrate and potassium chloride are made this way because the hydroxides and carbonates of sodium and potassium are soluble.
Link to topics: indicators and the pH scale are covered under 'pH and neutralisation'.
core.h: Making salts from soluble bases and alkalis (titration link)
core.p: If the base is **soluble**, such as sodium hydroxide, you cannot add it in excess and filter it off because it would dissolve. Instead the exact volumes needed to neutralise each other must be found by **titration** with an indicator. First the volume of alkali that neutralises the acid is found using an indicator; then the experiment is repeated without the indicator in the same volumes, because the indicator would contaminate the salt. Evaporation and crystallisation then give the salt. This distinction (insoluble base → filter, soluble alkali → titration) is a common exam question.

bullets: Suitable: magnesium, zinc, iron (reacting safely at a measurable rate).
Unsuitable: sodium, potassium, lithium, calcium (violent) and copper, silver, gold (no reaction).
Equation: Zn + H2SO4 → ZnSO4 + H2; Mg + 2HCl → MgCl2 + H2.
Hydrogen test: a lit splint makes a squeaky pop.
The metal is oxidised (loses electrons) and hydrogen ions are reduced; this is a redox reaction (Higher/triple link).
Ionic equation: Zn + 2H+ → Zn2+ + H2.
Reactivity series link: metals above hydrogen displace it from dilute acids; those below do not.
Keep the metal in excess so all the acid is used.
core.h: Which metals can be used, and why not all of them?
core.p: Metals can also make a soluble salt with an acid, but only if their reactivity is suitable. A very reactive metal such as sodium or potassium reacts explosively, so it would be dangerous. Metals less reactive than hydrogen, such as copper, silver and gold, do not react with dilute acids at all. A metal in the middle of the reactivity series, such as magnesium, zinc or iron, reacts at a moderate rate and so is suitable. Hydrogen gas is given off, and the metal is used in excess in the same way as the insoluble oxide.

bullets: Name the reactants: for example dilute sulfuric acid and copper oxide.
'Add the solid in small amounts / until in excess' and 'warm the acid'.
'Filter to remove the excess solid' - say what is left behind (residue) and what passes through (filtrate).
'Heat the filtrate in an evaporating basin to evaporate some of the water' (till crystals form on a glass rod).
'Leave to cool and crystallise' then 'filter and dry the crystals using filter paper'.
Give a reason for any step: 'excess to make sure all the acid has reacted'.
Include a safety point if asked: eye protection.
Level-of-response mark schemes reward a logical sequence even if one detail is missing.
core.h: Exam-style linking: what to write for a 6-mark answer
core.p: The 'describe how you would prepare a pure, dry sample of …' question is nearly always a 6 marker. To get full marks you must give the steps in the correct order and include a reason for each key step. Think of the answer as four stages: react, filter, evaporate, crystallise and dry. Also name the reagents, say that the solid is added in excess, state how you know the reaction is finished and mention the equipment. Marks are lost for vague words like 'heat it up' without saying only part of the water is evaporated.

exam: 1 mark: name the salt - say 'metal from the base' + 'ending from the acid' (chloride, nitrate, sulfate).
1 mark: 'to make sure all the acid has reacted' is the standard reason for adding excess solid.
2 marks: describe how to know the reaction is finished - 'some solid remains / no more solid dissolves / fizzing stops'.
2 marks: state what filtering removes (excess solid) and what is collected (filtrate).
3 marks: explain why you do not evaporate to dryness - spitting, powder not crystals, loss of water of crystallisation.
4 marks: give the order of steps correctly: react, filter, evaporate part, cool/crystallise, dry.
6 marks (level of response): include the reactants, the excess, filtering, evaporating until crystals form on a glass rod, cooling, drying and one safety point, in the correct order.
Word equations: use the pattern acid + base → salt + water, and add CO2 or H2 where relevant.
Symbol equation tip: balance the numbers last; sulfuric acid is H2SO4, nitric is HNO3, hydrochloric is HCl.
Calculations: always show moles = mass ÷ Mr, ratio from the equation, then mass = moles × Mr; give units (g) and sensible significant figures.

mistakes.r: Add the solid in excess (until some remains) so that all the acid has reacted; filter off the excess.
mistakes.w: Add just enough oxide until the solution turns blue.

mistakes.r: Heat gently to evaporate some of the water (until crystals form on a glass rod), then leave to cool and crystallise.
mistakes.w: Boil the solution until all the water has gone.

mistakes.r: Filtering removes the excess insoluble solid (residue); the salt passes through in the filtrate.
mistakes.w: Filtering removes the salt from the solution.

mistakes.r: Copper oxide is insoluble; it reacts with the acid to form soluble copper sulfate.
mistakes.w: Copper oxide is soluble so it dissolves.

mistakes.r: Copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series, so it does not react with dilute acids.
mistakes.w: Copper reacts with dilute sulfuric acid to make copper sulfate.

mistakes.r: Hydrochloric makes chlorides, sulfuric makes sulfates and nitric makes nitrates.
Sodium hydroxide is soluble, so you cannot filter it off; use a titration with an indicator instead.
mistakes.w: Using sodium hydroxide in excess and filtering.

mistakes.r: Carbonates produce carbon dioxide (turns limewater cloudy); metals produce hydrogen (squeaky pop).

summary: You must know how a pure, dry sample of a soluble salt is made from an acid and an insoluble solid (metal, oxide, hydroxide or carbonate): add the solid in excess, filter off the leftover, then crystallise the salt solution. This is an AQA required practical, so you need to describe the method, explain why each step is done, name the salt that forms and write the equation. It is a classic 6-mark 'describe how' question.

terms.d: A compound formed when the hydrogen in an acid is replaced by a metal or ammonium ion.
Able to dissolve in a solvent, such as water, to form a solution.
Unable to dissolve in a solvent; it stays as a solid.
A substance that reacts with an acid to neutralise it, forming a salt and water; e.g. metal oxides, hydroxides, carbonates.
A base that dissolves in water, forming a solution with a pH above 7 containing hydroxide ions.
A reaction between an acid and a base that forms a salt and water (the acid's H+ ions react with OH- ions).
More of a reactant than is needed, so some is left over when the reaction has finished.
The liquid that passes through filter paper during filtration.
The solid that remains on the filter paper after filtering.
A process in which a solid forms crystals from a saturated solution as the solvent evaporates or the solution cools.
A solution in which no more solute can dissolve at that temperature.
Water molecules that are chemically part of the crystal structure, e.g. the 5H2O in CuSO4.5H2O.
A crystal that contains water of crystallisation.
The reactant that is completely used up first and so limits the amount of product formed.
The actual mass of product made divided by the theoretical mass possible, multiplied by 100.

worked.ans: Model answer: react warm dilute sulfuric acid with excess zinc oxide, filter to remove the unreacted oxide, evaporate part of the water until the point of crystallisation, cool to crystallise, filter and dry the zinc sulfate crystals. Equation: ZnO + H2SO4 → ZnSO4 + H2O.
worked.q: Describe how you would make a pure, dry sample of zinc sulfate crystals from zinc oxide and dilute sulfuric acid. (6 marks)
steps: Warm the dilute sulfuric acid in a beaker (do not boil).
Add zinc oxide a little at a time, stirring, until it stops dissolving and some is left over (excess), so that all the acid has reacted.
Filter the mixture to remove the excess zinc oxide (residue); the zinc sulfate solution is the filtrate.
Pour the filtrate into an evaporating basin and heat gently to evaporate some of the water until crystals start to form on a glass rod (the point of crystallisation).
Leave the solution to cool slowly so crystals form.
Filter off the crystals, rinse with a little cold distilled water and dry with filter paper or in a warm oven.
